text: You're given n points on a 2D plane. The cost to connect any two points is their Manhattan distance. Return the minimum total cost to connect all points, so every point can reach every other point.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I can connect any pair of points, and the cost of that edge is fixed: the Manhattan distance between them. I want every point connected into one piece, for the least total cost. Is that right?

Then the key observation is this: I have a complete graph. Every pair of points is an edge, weighted by its Manhattan distance. Connecting all points for the least total cost, with no wasted edges, is exactly the definition of a minimum spanning tree. So the answer is the weight of the MST, and it uses exactly n minus one edges. Are there any constraints on the input size?
n is up to a thousand. Coordinates fit in an int.

Let me run through the example: five points — zero zero, two two, three ten, five two, and seven zero. The cheapest wiring uses P1 to P3 at three, P0 to P1 at four, P3 to P4 at four, and P1 to P2 at nine. That sums to twenty, which matches the expected answer.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to try every subset of edges that connects all points and keep the cheapest. But the number of subsets explodes, so that's not feasible. This problem reminds me of the two classic minimum spanning tree algorithms: Prim's and Kruskal's. Both are greedy, and both give a provably minimum tree. I'll show both — they solve the same problem from two angles.

Here's the plan for both. One: Prim grows a tree from point zero with a min-heap, always taking the cheapest edge to a new node. Two: Kruskal pops all pair edges from the smallest up, and Union-Find drops any edge whose endpoints are already connected. Three: stop at n nodes for Prim, or n minus one edges for Kruskal. One thing worth flagging — greedy is safe because of the cut property: for any split of the points into two groups, the cheapest crossing edge belongs to some MST. Prim uses the cut tree versus outside; Kruskal uses it each time it joins two blocks. Both cost n squared log n on this dense graph. Array-based Prim gets n squared, but the heap versions are cleaner and fast enough for a thousand points. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Code them both up.

Alright, let me code this up. Prim first: a min-heap of weight and node, seeded with point zero at cost zero. Each fresh pop adds a node to the tree and pushes its edges to every outside node. One thing worth flagging — the line that skips a node already in the tree is required, not an optimization. The same node gets pushed many times with different weights; the first pop settles it, and every later pop is stale and would double-count edges. Then Kruskal: push every pair edge into a min-heap by weight, and pop until I've added n minus one edges. Here, Union returning false is the cycle check — both endpoints already share a root, so I drop that edge. Only a true, a real merge, adds to the total.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. I'll trace Kruskal on the five points, since its edge-by-edge view is easy to follow. Expected output is twenty. The row that matters is the nine: the three weight-seven edges were all skipped because their endpoints were already connected, so the far-off point three, ten joins last through P1 to P2. That's the fourth edge, n minus one, so the total is twenty and the loop stops. Corner cases: a single point returns zero, since Kruskal's loop never runs. The second example, three twelve, minus two five, minus four one, gives eighteen. Negative coordinates are fine, because Manhattan distance uses abs.

Time is n squared log n for both. The graph is complete, so there are about n squared over two edges, and each heap operation costs a log. Space is n squared, since both can hold that many edges in the heap. In the worst case, with n equal to a thousand, that's about half a million edges — well within limits. Oh, one more thing — if n were much larger, pushing all those edges would be wasteful. The clean fix for a dense graph is array-based Prim: keep the cheapest distance to each outside node in a plain array, and pick the minimum each round in linear time, with no heap at all. That's n squared time and linear space.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You reframed connecting all points cheaply as an MST on a complete graph right away, instead of reaching for shortest paths. You named the cut property as the reason both greedy algorithms are correct, not just that they work. And you flagged the lazy skip in Prim and the cycle check in Kruskal as correctness requirements, then gave the n squared dense-graph fix unprompted. Good work.
